item.title: TIMES SHOPPER | Shankar’s secret to family savings
item.description: FOR 41-year-old David Shankar, a successful shopping trip begins long before he walks through the supermarket doors. Armed with a carefully prepared shopping list and a clear budget, the Visama resident believes planning is the key to keeping his family happy, healthy, and financially secure.
item.content:encoded:
FOR 41-year-old David Shankar, a successful shopping trip begins long before he walks through the supermarket doors.

Armed with a carefully prepared shopping list and a clear budget, the Visama resident believes planning is the key to keeping his family happy, healthy, and financially secure.

As a regular customer of Pac N Save Nausori, Shankar has developed a shopping routine that helps him manage the needs of his growing household while navigating the challenges of rising living costs.

Living with his wife, two children, and his mother, Shankar carries the responsibility of being the family’s primary breadwinner.

While balancing work and family life can be demanding, he says providing the best for his loved ones remains his top priority.

In today’s economic climate, he believes every dollar counts.

“With the increase in fuel prices and the rising cost of living, families need to be more careful about how they spend their money,” Shankar says.

“We need to be prepared whenever we go shopping and make sure we budget properly.”

For him, one simple habit makes all the difference creating a shopping list before leaving home.

“Preparing before doing your shopping is the major key for all shoppers,” he explains.

“We should always have a list, so we know exactly what we need to buy. Many people forget important items and end up making extra trips back to the shop. A shopping list helps you stay organised and avoid unnecessary spending.

Over the years, Pac N Save Nausori has become Shankar’s preferred supermarket for household groceries and essentials.

He says the combination of quality products, affordable prices, and dependable service keeps him coming back.

“When it comes to shopping for my family, Pac N Save never lets me down,” he says.

“I have been shopping here for quite some time, and what I appreciate most is that the prices are always reasonable and consistent.

For a father responsible for providing for a large household, consistency matters. Knowing that he can rely on fair pricing allows him to plan his family’s budget with confidence.

“In some supermarkets, prices can fluctuate a lot, but here I know what to expect,” he says.

“The weekly specials also make a real difference because they help families save money on everyday items.”

Every fortnight, Shankar sets aside approximately $390 for groceries. However, like many families, unexpected needs sometimes arise between major shopping trips.

“My shopping budget is usually around $390 every fortnight, but if we run short of groceries, we stop by town and pick up the things we need to replace at home.”

Despite the challenges of managing household expenses, Shankar believes smart shopping is about much more than saving money. For him, it is about ensuring his family enjoys a comfortable and healthy lifestyle.

“Shopping for a family requires planning, you need to take your time, compare prices, and make the best choices because life is becoming more expensive every day.”

Whether he is shopping for fresh produce, household necessities, or items for his children, Shankar carefully considers every purchase. His goal is always to maximise value without compromising on quality.

As a loyal customer, he also appreciates the variety available at Pac N Save Nausori, which allows him to complete most of his shopping in one convenient location.

“The supermarket has a wide range of products, and that makes shopping easier for families like mine.

“You can find what you need without having to visit multiple stores.”

For Shankar, successful shopping is not about spending more it is about spending wisely. Through careful planning, disciplined budgeting, and smart purchasing decisions, he continues to provide for the people who matter most.

His advice to other shoppers is simple but powerful.

“My message to the people of Nausori is to come and do your shopping at Pac N Save Supermarket,” he says.

“You will save money, find a great variety of products, and get quality goods for your family. With proper planning and smart shopping, every family can make their budget go further.”

item.content:encoded:
Bula vinaka everyone, Last weekend I drove to the carwash in Nadawa, only to find it closed. The place has recently become a target for police attention because of alleged illegal activities in the vicinity.

I was told by the operators that when the electricity bill went up, the carwash had little choice but to increase their prices. A general wash that previously cost $15 went up by another $10 to $25.

For many customers, that was simply too much, and the business lost a good number of them. So, I headed to another carwash at the back of a service station in Laucala Beach Estate. I was told that what used to cost $15 had also gone up to $25.

As I waited, a well-known architect arrived with a stockbroker, and the two men chatted while their cars were being washed. I joined them in conversation.

Our discussion soon drifted from how Fiji faces a severe non-communicable disease (NCD) crisis, with cardiovascular disease (including heart attacks) remaining the country’s biggest killer and diabetes driving an alarming rate of 3 to 5 lower-limb amputations daily (roughly one every 8 to 12 hours), to the rising cost of living and the growing pressure families are facing as they try to make ends meet.

The conversation was a reminder that behind every increase in the price of fuel, electricity, food, transport or services is a family trying to stretch an already tight household budget.

While for some, an extra $10 may seem manageable, for others, it could mean a loaf of bread, a few vegetables, bus fare, school expenses or something needed at home. When the gentlemen left, I turned my attention to the two women who were busy washing cars.

Their conversation brought home another side of the economic struggle — the importance of women earning an income to keep their families going. As they worked, they shared their personal stories with me. Both women said their husbands had left home, leaving them to fend for their children.

Car washing is hard work at the best of times, but it is particularly difficult for women during this cold season and more so for young mothers. One of the women had only recently recovered from illness. The other has a six-month-old baby at home, being looked after by her mother while she works.

Both women were working because they had families to support and even though it was tough they still had to turn up. And that, for me, was an eye opener from my visit to the carwash. We often talk about the cost of living in terms of statistics, inflation rates and household spending.

But the real story is found in places like this where people work hard to earn $5.30 an hour for their children. It is in the mother leaving her six-month-old baby with her own mother so she can earn a day’s income.

It is in the woman returning to work after recovering from illness because her children still need food and school expenses paid. It is in the family deciding whether to spend $25 washing the car or use that money for something more important.

These are the everyday calculations many Fijian families are making today. For households already struggling, every price increase adds another layer of pressure.

And while some people can absorb a $10 increase without much thought, there are families for whom $10 matters enormously. The two women at the carwash show that behind every price tag is a human story.

It is usually a story of pain, hard work, struggles and sacrifice. Sometimes, it is a story of survival. And often, it is a story of mothers doing whatever work they can find to put food on the table and keep their families moving forward during these hard times.

So, the next time we complain, spare a thought for those who have no room left in their budgets to absorb another increase. For many families, there is simply nowhere else to cut. That is the reality of the cost-of-living struggle in Fiji today.

Food for thought everyone and spend wisely this weekend, but even better help someone you can!

item.title: MOTORING & ACCESSORIES | Family drives Kumar to go on
item.description: FOR 16 years, Michael Kumar has been a familiar face at the Tebara Complex taxi base in Nakasi, Nausori greeting passengers with a smile and ensuring they reach their destinations safely. While what he earns helps pay the bills, the 52-year-old says there is one thing that motivates him more than anything else — his family.
item.content:encoded:
FOR 16 years, Michael Kumar has been a familiar face at the Tebara Complex taxi base in Nakasi, Nausori greeting passengers with a smile and ensuring they reach their destinations safely.

While what he earns helps pay the bills, the 52-year-old says there is one thing that motivates him more than anything else — his family.

Living in Davuilevu Housing with his wife, three children and elderly parents, Kumar says every day behind the wheel is about providing for the people who depend on him.

“Driving a taxi is my job, and it allows me to support my children and also take care of my parents. That is what keeps me going every day.” Kumar starts work at 8am and usually finishes by 6pm.

Unlike many drivers who work late into the night, he prefers daylight hours, believing it is safer for both him and his passengers.

“I don’t like driving at night because of safety concerns,” he explained.

“My regular customers know my schedule, and many of them have been travelling with me for years.”

His friendly nature and dependable service have earned him the trust of passengers, many of whom request him by name.

Over the years, however, Kumar has witnessed significant changes in the taxi industry.

Rising fuel prices, increasing vehicle maintenance costs and the higher cost of living have made it difficult for many drivers to stay on the road.

“There were around 21 taxidrivers operating from this base,” he said.

“Now, only a few of us are still running regularly because business has slowed down and operating costs continue to increase.”

Another growing challenge is competition from private vehicles and unlicensed transport operators, who often collect passengers close to taxi stands.

“Private vehicles are taking many of our customers,” Kumar said.

“They wait near our base and pick people up before they reach us.

“It makes it harder for taxidrivers who depend on this work every day.”

Competition among taxi operators has also intensified, with several taxi bases now operating throughout Nakasi.

“There are many taxi stands in the area, so we’re all competing for the same passengers,” he said.

“It’s not easy, but we keep working because our families depend on us.”

Despite the challenges, Kumar remains committed to delivering quality service. He believes taxi driving is not only about transporting passengers from one place to another, but about building trust, ensuring safety and treating every customer with respect.

“Our passengers should always come first,” he said.

“We have a responsibility to make them feel safe and comfortable. Good customer service is what keeps people coming back.”

Reflecting on his years behind the wheel, Kumar says the profession has taught him patience, resilience and the value of honest work.

For those considering a career as a taxidriver, he offers simple but meaningful advice.

“You have to enjoy what you do, be confident, be respectful and be prepared to work hard. Success doesn’t come easily, but if you’re committed and willing to serve people with a positive attitude, you can build a good life.”

After more than 16 years on the road, Kumar continues to drive with purpose proving that every journey he makes is ultimately one that leads back to the people he loves most.

item.description: IN today’s economic climate, where the cost of living continues to rise and every dollar matters, many Fijian families are finding creative ways to stretch their household budgets without compromising on nutrition. For 44-year-old Tamara Thomas Turagasau, smart shopping is not just about finding the lowest prices, it’s about making informed choices that keep her family healthy while ensuring every
item.content:encoded:
IN today’s economic climate, where the cost of living continues to rise and every dollar matters, many Fijian families are finding creative ways to stretch their household budgets without compromising on nutrition.

For 44-year-old Tamara Thomas Turagasau, smart shopping is not just about finding the lowest prices, it’s about making informed choices that keep her family healthy while ensuring every shopping trip delivers real value.

Originally from Tubou, Lakeba, Lau and with maternal links to Rotuma, Tamara now calls Tacirua home.

Together with her husband and their two growing sons, she has developed a practical shopping routine that helps her family navigate rising food and fuel costs while maintaining a balanced lifestyle.

For Tamara, the family’s grocery journey almost always begins at Extra Supermarket, Laucala Beach, a store she has come to trust for its combination of affordability, convenience and quality.

“Most of our weekly shopping is done at Extra Supermarket Laucala Beach,” she says.

“The prices are reasonable compared to some supermarkets that are supposed to be more budget friendly.”

Every fortnight, Tamara carefully plans her grocery budget, setting aside between $250 and $300 for household essentials.

Rather than shopping on impulse, she enters the supermarket with a clear plan focused on feeding her family nutritious meals.

The shopping trolley is first filled with everyday necessities such as rice, sugar and bread before moving on to fresh produce and protein.

“Because we have growing children, we always make sure there are plenty of fruits and vegetables, together with fish and chicken.

For Tamara, healthy eating is an investment in her family’s future. She believes nutritious meals help her children stay active, healthy and ready for school while encouraging lifelong eating habits built around fresh, wholesome foods.

Like thousands of families across Fiji, Tamara has felt the impact of increasing food prices and higher fuel costs.

But instead of letting these challenges overwhelm the family budget, she has adjusted her shopping habits by making greater use of Fiji’s local markets.

“We manage by keeping to local fresh fruits and vegetables from the market,” she says.

Regular market visits have become an important part of her family’s shopping routine. Spending around $150 each visit, Tamara buys fresh cabbage, carrots, pumpkin, spinach, ota, fresh fish and other seasonal produce that not only costs less but also provide excellent nutritional value.

By combining supermarket shopping with fresh market produce, Tamara has found a balance that allows her family to enjoy healthy meals while supporting local farmers and market vendors.

It’s a strategy that keeps costs under control while ensuring fresh ingredients remain on the family menu.

Her approach demonstrates that successful budgeting isn’t about sacrificing quality it is about planning ahead, comparing prices and making thoughtful purchasing decisions.

Every shopping trip is guided by what the family truly needs rather than unnecessary extras. Tamara believes families can still eat well despite economic pressures, provided they remain disciplined and flexible with their spending.

Her message to other shoppers is refreshingly simple but deeply relevant.

“Work with what you can afford and choose the healthier options that are available.”

Through thoughtful choices, a well-planned shopping list and a focus on fresh local produce, Tamara Thomas Turagasau proves that feeding a family well doesn’t always require spending more, it simply requires shopping smarter.

item.title: TIMES SHOPPER | Make better choices at the supermarket
item.description: HEALTHY eating begins long before food reaches your plate it starts at the supermarket. Knowing how to choose nutritious foods can make shopping easier, faster, and even more affordable.
item.content:encoded:
HEALTHY eating begins long before food reaches your plate it starts at the supermarket.

Knowing how to choose nutritious foods can make shopping easier, faster, and even more affordable.

By planning ahead and understanding food labels, you can fill your trolley with wholesome ingredients while avoiding unnecessary purchases.

A few simple habits can help you build healthier meals, save money, and support your long-term wellbeing.

One of the most effective ways to shop smart is to plan your meals and snacks for the week before you leave home.

Preparing a shopping list based on your meal plan ensures that you buy everything you need while reducing impulse purchases.

Sticking to your list also helps you stay within your budget and prevents food waste. Another useful tip is to avoid shopping when you are hungry, as this can make tempting, less healthy foods harder to resist.

When shopping, focus on choosing foods from the five major food groups vegetables and legumes, fruits, wholegrain cereals, lean proteins, and dairy or suitable alternatives.

These foods provide the essential nutrients your body needs for good health. Try to limit discretionary foods such as chips, confectionery, sugary drinks, pastries, and processed snacks, which are often high in added sugars, unhealthy fats, and salt.

Reading food labels is an important skill that helps you compare products and choose healthier options.

Pay attention to the nutrition information panel and ingredient list, looking for products that are lower in sodium, saturated fat, and added sugars while being higher in fibre and whole grains.

Dried legumes such as lentils, chickpeas, and beans, along with grains like barley, bulgur, and couscous, are excellent pantry staples.

They are affordable, nutritious, and naturally low in salt. These foods are rich in fibre and plant-based protein, making them ideal for soups, salads, and main meals.

While canned soups are convenient, many contain high levels of sodium.

Preparing homemade soups allows you to control the amount of salt and include plenty of fresh vegetables.

Canned vegetables and fish can also be healthy choices when selected carefully.

Choose vegetables, including tomatoes, corn, and legumes, that are canned without added salt.

For canned fish such as salmon, tuna, and sardines, compare labels and select products with lower sodium levels.

These foods provide valuable protein and healthy fats while being convenient and affordable.

For staple carbohydrates, choose wholemeal pasta and brown rice instead of refined varieties.

Whole grains contain more fibre, vitamins, and minerals, helping you stay fuller for longer.

Avoid ready-made pasta, rice meals, and meal bases, as they are often high in added salt.

When buying pasta sauces, compare labels and select those with lower sodium.

Breakfast cereals can vary greatly in their nutritional value.

Choose wholegrain varieties that are high in fibre and lower in added sugars and salt.

If you enjoy muesli and are watching your weight, keep portion sizes moderate, as these cereals are more energy dense.

In the dairy section, choose reduced-fat milk, yoghurt, and cheese where possible. Look for cheeses containing 15 grams of fat or less per 100 grams and yoghurts that are low in fat and added sugar.

Reduced-fat dairy products provide calcium and protein while containing fewer kilojoules.

You can also make homemade custards and milk desserts using low-fat milk and less added sugar.

Evaporated skim milk is a healthier substitute for cream in many recipes, while reduced-fat polyunsaturated spreads are a better choice than butter for those aiming to reduce their energy intake.
